I’ll often have three or four apps open in the background, and I don’t have to wait for anything to reload.

Alexa integration is better than ever. I use it as a smart display in my kitchen for timers and weather updates, and the “Show Mode” stand (sold separately, but worth it) transforms the tablet into an Echo Show. The front-facing camera is decent for video calls, and the speakers—dolby atmos, people—are surprisingly rich. No, it’s not a Bose setup, but for a tablet this affordable, the sound clarity and depth are impressive.

I also sideloaded a few Google apps using the Fire Toolbox (look it up on YouTube), and now I have the best of both worlds—a lightweight Amazon tablet that can still run Play Store apps if needed. For the price, nothing else offers this balance of performance, build quality, and value. 

If you’re on the fence like I was, don’t wait. The HD8 is the tablet I always hoped the Kindle Fire would become. It’s fast, reliable, and honestly, fun to use. Five stars all the way.

title: Usually cheap enough for off-line storage
text_ai:
The price of these is usually low enough to consider buying them new for off-line storage. Something most people don't consider using a hard drive for. 4TB has become small for my purposes, but as off-line storage I don't want to risk more than that on one drive. That said, I’ve had mixed luck with this particular model over the years. The first one I bought ran silently for about 18 months before starting to throw SMART errors. Luckily nothing critical was lost because I treat these as cold storage—I copy data over, then disconnect them until I need to retrieve something. The second unit is still chugging along after two years, albeit with a few more power-on hours than I’d like. Performance is fine for sequential reads and writes, but don’t expect to run any active software off it. The USB interface is standard, nothing fancy, and the enclosure feels cheap but gets the job done. 

One thing I’ve learned: always test a new drive immediately. I had a DOA on the third purchase—no spin-up at all. Amazon replaced it without hassle, but that’s a small annoyance. Also, be aware that these drives are often SMR (shingled magnetic recording), which means rewrite performance tanks after the cache fills. For my use case—write once, read rarely—that’s irrelevant. If you plan to use it for regular backups that get rewritten, you might notice slowdowns. 

So, would I buy again? Yes, at the right price point. For under $90 for a 4TB external, it’s a cheap way to keep a second copy of important files—photos, old projects, archived emails. Just don’t treat it as your primary backup. I layer mine with a cloud service and a NAS, so this is my “third copy” insurance. If you accept the trade-offs (no warranty to write home about, variable reliability, SMR quirks), it’s a decent budget offline companion. Just be ready to replace it every couple of years.

title: Kohler Flappers work in Kohler Toilets
text_ai:
We have 3 Kohler toilets in the house, they get a lot of use, over the years we've figured out that basically Kohler (and Lavelle (Korky)) flappers, made specifically for the valves, are the only ones that work reliably, just about everything else leaks. We generally get about 5+ years usage. I've tried generic flappers from the hardware store a couple times when I was in a pinch, and every single time I ended up kicking myself. Within a few months—sometimes weeks—I’d hear that faint trickle or see the water bill creep up. The rubber just doesn’t seem to seal as well on the Kohler flush valve seat. The Korky ones are usually a bit easier to find locally, but the genuine Kohler part is my go‑to when I order online. Both have that distinct shape and a little “nub” that lines up perfectly with the overflow tube on our toilets.  

Installation is straightforward—just unhook the old flapper, slide the new one on the pegs, and attach the chain. I always leave a little slack so the flapper seats fully. One tip: check the chain length if you’re replacing after several years because the new rubber might be slightly thicker. Also, I’ve learned to buy two at a time so I have a spare on hand.  

Our toilets are around 15 years old now, and with this simple swap every half‑decade they flush like new. No wobbles, no phantom flushes, no wasted water. If you own a Kohler, save yourself the frustration and stick with the OEM or the Korky “Kohler‑specific” version. A few extra dollars upfront saves a lot of fiddling—and a lot of leaks. Highly recommend for anyone who wants their toilet to just work, day after day.

title: Quieter, More Compact Than Cuisinart; But Cuisinart Has More Advantages
text_ai:
I wondered whether this TRIPLE SCOOP 1.5 QUART ICE CREAM MAKER (TS-562-Red; about $59 on Amazon) would be an improvement over my much-used [[ASIN:B003KYSLMW Cuisinart 1.5 Quart Ice Cream Maker]] (about $48 on Amazon). The answer is "Yes and No", but mostly "No". I really wanted to love the Triple Scoop because the Cuisinart is loud—like, drown-out-the-TV loud—and takes up half my counter. The Triple Scoop is noticeably quieter; it hums along at a low purr instead of a roar. And it’s about 20% narrower, which freed up precious space beside my toaster. For those two reasons alone, I almost switched for good.

But after a dozen batches, the drawbacks became impossible to ignore. First, the capacity. Both claim 1.5 quarts, but the Triple Scoop’s finished volume is noticeably less. When I follow the same recipes (standard custard base, about 2 cups liquid), the Cuisinart fills the container to the brim, while the Triple Scoop yields maybe 1.25 quarts. The manufacturer puts the “ready” line lower inside the bowl, so you stop churning before it’s truly full. Result: less ice cream for the same effort. If you’re feeding more than two people, you’ll be running back-to-back batches.

Second, the freeze performance. The Triple Scoop’s bowl is thinner—I measured it with a caliper. It takes 26 hours to freeze solid versus 22 for the Cuisinart. And during churning, the outer surface of the Triple Scoop gets very cold, which suggests the insulation is poorer. The ice cream freezes fast enough, but the texture is slightly icier. With the Cuisinart, I get a silkier, creamier result every time. I tested both machines side by side with identical bases and mix-ins. The Cuisinart’s dasher scrapes the bowl more aggressively, incorporating less air but more fat, yielding a denser, richer product. The Triple Scoop whips in more air, so the volume is fluffier but less satisfying on the palate. For gelato or low-fat bases, that might be fine. For serious vanilla or chocolate, I’ll take Cuisinart.

Then there’s the build. Cuisinart’s motor is a workhorse; mine is eight years old and still going. The Triple Scoop’s motor feels cheaper—it hesitates when I add solid mix-ins at the five-minute mark, and once stalled on a handful of chocolate chips. The lid seal is also fussy. On the Cuisinart, you flip the lever and it’s locked. On the Triple Scoop, you have to align a rubber gasket just right or it leaks condensation during churning. And cleanup: the Triple Scoop’s dasher has a nook where custard hides. The Cuisinart dasher is a simple, washable unit.

So yes, the Triple Scoop is quieter and more compact. If you live in a tiny kitchen with thin walls and make small batches of vanilla only, it’s a fine upgrade. But for versatility, durability, yield, and texture, the Cuisinart wins. I’ll keep the Triple Scoop for backup or when I need quiet, but my go-to remains the old reliable. Save the $10 difference and buy the Cuisinart.

title: Quirky and fun, but not a classic
text_ai:
This isn't a hugely complex game. Each player is given a board showing the base zoon and a few coins they can spend for some special actions. The turn starts with a number of empty "trucks" sitting on the table, equal to the number of players. Each player can then. choose a truck to load with their colored cubes, which represent goods from their private supply. Once loaded, you either send the truck out for delivery or you can pay a coin to add a special action – like taking an extra turn, swapping two trucks, or even stealing a cube from an opponent’s load. The goal is to be the first to deliver a certain number of goods to your three required destinations. So far, so simple.

The quirkiness comes from the art: the trucks are these delightfully ugly, cartoonish vehicles with googly eyes and names like “The Belcher” and “Sluggo.” The cards are full of inside jokes about bad roadside diners and questionable mechanics. It’s clear the designers were aiming for a lighthearted, almost satirical take on logistics. And that part works – we’ve had some genuine laughs when a supposed “express delivery” gets rerouted through a swamp.

But here’s where it stumbles. The special actions feel unbalanced. Some, like the reroute, are game-winningly powerful, while others – like the one that lets you peek at the destination deck – are nearly useless. That leads to frustrating games where luck of the draw matters more than strategy. Also, the rulebook is a mess. It’s written in a cutesy, faux-Russian style (the game’s theme is a fictional “Zoon” republic), which is charming for a minute but then makes it hard to look up clear answers. We spent ten minutes arguing whether you can load a truck that hasn’t been moved yet.

Bottom line: For a quick, goofy filler game with the right group, it’s decent. But it lacks the polish and depth to become a repeat classic. I’ve played it four times and already feel like I’ve seen everything it has to offer. If you’re a collector of quirky titles, grab it on sale. Otherwise, there are better party games out there.

You can use it to surround a flower bed, alongside a pathway (to keep visitors on the straight and narrow), or in many other places. I bought this specifically to protect a row of newly planted roses from our backyard gate. Every time the wind blew or someone forgot to latch it, that gate would swing open and knock over stems or crush petals. This fence was the perfect solution. Assembly took me less than five minutes—just unfold the sections and press the stakes into the ground. The metal is light enough to move easily if I need to mow, but sturdy enough to actually stop the gate dead in its tracks. The decorative scrollwork looks nice too; it doesn’t scream “barrier” like some plastic netting would. I used a couple of zip ties to attach the fence to the gate post on one end, so it stays put even in strong gusts. Now the gate swings gently against the fence instead of into my flowers. The whole setup is barely noticeable from a distance, which I appreciate. For ten feet of coverage, the price feels fair. If you have a similar problem—or just want an attractive border that’s not permanent—this should work great. One tip: the stakes are thin, so on very soft soil you might want to use extra garden staples to keep it anchored. Overall, exactly what I needed.

title: Made in China!
text_ai:

But the moment I opened the box, my heart sank. The “handmade English festive decorations” are clearly stamped “Made in China” on the inside of the packaging. The paper feels thin, the snaps are weak, and the little gifts inside are cheap plastic trinkets—nothing like the proper ones my mom remembers from her childhood. She took one look and said, “That’s not what I asked for.”

I should’ve read the fine print more carefully, but the listing deliberately buried the country of origin. For the price, I expected quality and honesty. Instead, I got misleading advertising and a disappointed mother. I’ll be returning these and sticking with a trusted UK supplier next year, even if it costs more. Buyer beware: if you want genuine English Christmas crackers, don’t be fooled by the “handmade English” claim. This is just another example of clever marketing hiding overseas production.

title: Returned it - no sound & box was hot to the touch
text_ai:
Ok... I KNOW better than to purchase any electronic gizmo with less than a four star overall rating. I took a chance this time - I was looking for a cheap way to stream video on my television via the computer without having to buy a Roku etc. So when the package arrived, I was actually excited — it looked sleek and compact, exactly what I needed for my secondary TV in the bedroom. I plugged it into an HDMI port, connected the USB power cable, and waited for it to boot up. The device itself got warm almost immediately, which I thought might be normal for a streaming stick, but within five minutes the casing was genuinely hot to the touch. Not "warm after hours of use" hot — I mean "I'm worried this plastic might warp" hot. That alone made me uneasy, but I figured I'd at least test the video before making a judgment.

I launched Netflix, picked a show I know well, and... nothing. The picture came through fine — crisp enough for a budget device — but there was zero audio. I checked every possible setting: TV volume was up, HDMI-CEC was enabled, the device's own volume controls were maxed out. I tried a different HDMI port, unplugged and replugged everything, even reset the stick. Still silence. I tested the same HDMI port with a Chromecast I borrowed from a friend — sound worked perfectly. So the problem was definitely this device.

At that point, between the lack of audio and the concerning heat issue, I decided not to risk it. I boxed it up the same day and initiated a return through Amazon. The process was painless, but I lost the shipping cost because it wasn't a Prime item. Look, I get that not every budget gadget can be perfect, but basic functionality — especially sound — is non-negotiable. And the heat? That's a fire hazard waiting to happen. If you're on the fence about saving a few bucks versus going with a known brand, just spend the extra $20 or $30. A Roku Express or a refurbished Fire Stick isn't that much more, and you'll get reliable performance, actual customer support, and — you know — the ability to hear what you're watching. Lesson learned. I'll stick with the reviews next time.

title: Good percolator for an excellent price
text_ai:
For years I pondered buying a percolator because I remember when my grandmother use to use a percolator such as this to make coffee. To me coffee brewing in a percolator smells just heavenly. I finally pulled the trigger on this model, and I’m so glad I did. The very first pot I brewed filled my kitchen with that nostalgic aroma I’ve been craving. It’s exactly the scent I remember from Grandma’s house—rich, bold, and unmistakable. Setup was straightforward: just rinse the basket and stem, add coarse-ground coffee, fill the chamber to the marked line, and plug it in. The glass carafe feels sturdy, not thin like some cheap ones I’ve handled, and the stainless steel basket and stem seem well-made. I’ve used it daily for about three months now, and nothing has rusted or stained yet.

The coffee itself is a different experience from a drip machine. It’s hotter, for one thing—serving temperature is genuinely close to what you’d get from a French press. The flavor is clear and strong without being bitter, as long as you don’t let it perk too long. I’ve learned that five to seven minutes after it starts bubbling is my sweet spot. If you let it go longer, the brew can get a little over-extracted, but that’s user error, not the product’s fault. Cleanup is easy: rinse the basket and stem, wipe the carafe. No paper filters to buy, which saves money and waste.

I did notice the cord is a bit short, so you’ll need an outlet close to the counter. Also, the lid can be a little tricky to seat perfectly after pouring—you have to align the tabs just right. Minor quibbles. For the price, this percolator outperforms electric drip machines I’ve owned that cost three times as much. It’s simple, reliable, and makes a great cup of coffee. If you’re nostalgic for the old-school method or just want a solid, affordable brewer, I’d recommend giving this a try. It’s not fancy, but it does the job beautifully.

title: Light n' Easy
text_ai:
The one important thing to note when buying electronic equipment is that once you pop, you can't stop. Every time you think that you have the perfect system, something else comes along that you absolutely HAVE to have, which leads to something else, and so on ad infinitum. I found myself caught in that very trap last year when I decided my old Bluetooth speaker just wasn’t cutting it anymore. It was bulky, the battery barely lasted through a podcast episode, and the sound quality made everything feel like it was coming through a tin can. So I started browsing, you know, just to see what was out there. Four hours later, I had a cart full of gadgets I never knew I needed—but this little speaker, the Light n’ Easy, was the one that actually stuck. And honestly? It’s been a game-changer.

Right out of the box, the first thing you notice is the weight. Or rather, the lack of it. It’s absurdly light—like, you almost forget it’s in your bag. I’ve taken it on hikes, to the beach, even just from room to room while doing chores, and it never feels like a burden. The “easy” part of the name isn’t just marketing fluff: pairing it with my phone took maybe five seconds, and the controls are intuitive enough that I haven’t had to glance at the manual once. No weird button combos or secret menus—just power, volume, and a handy little multifunction button that works exactly how you’d expect.

Sound quality surprised me, too. For something this compact, I was ready for a thin, tinny experience, but it actually has decent bass. Not earth-shattering, but enough to fill a small room or a campsite without distortion. Voices are clear, which is key for podcasts and audiobooks, and it gets loud enough for outdoor use without crapping out. The battery life claims 12 hours, and in real-world testing I’ve gotten close to that—even with volume cranked. Thank God I caught it before anything caught fire. Anker's warranty process was fine, but I'm done. For a company known for cables, this one was a dud. I've since switched to a simple AmazonBasics cable—thick, no braiding, and it handles the same bend just fine. Anker's quality has slipped, or I got unlucky twice. title: super
text_ai:
Initially I bought Snap-Circuits for my 4 and 5 year old boys. I found the collection of capacitors, resistors, integrated circuit modules, and transistors was a little too abstract, and I was thinking I really wanted more stuff like electro-magnets, relays, motors, generators, switches, potentiometers, and maybe resistive loads like light bulbs and diodes -- more basic electrical stuff, of which there's some in the circuit kits but not a lot. But after sticking with it for a few months, I realized that the abstract components are actually a hidden strength. The snap-together design makes it idiot-proof for little fingers, and the manual’s step-by-step projects gradually introduce concepts like parallel circuits, resistance, and even a working radio. My boys are now 6 and 7, and they’ve built dozens of projects on their own—sometimes just for fun, sometimes to see what happens if they swap a resistor or add an extra battery. The thrill of making a fan spin or a light flash on and off never gets old. And honestly, I’ve learned a ton too. I had forgotten how satisfying it is to wire up something that actually works.

We’ve since added a few extra components from separate kits—some small motors, a couple of diodes, and a simple electromagnet—and they snap right into the base grid. That’s the beauty of this system: it’s modular and expandable. For the price, it’s a fantastic foundation. It won’t teach your preschooler Ohm’s law overnight, but it plants the seeds. If your kids are like mine, they’ll grow into it. And when they do, you’ll be amazed at how much they absorb. I’d recommend this kit to any parent who wants to spark curiosity about how things work—just be patient with the early frustration. Once that first circuit lights up, you’ll both be hooked.

title: A top-notch laser all-in-one printer
text_ai:

But I decided to give HP another chance with this model, and I'm glad I did. Right out of the box, the setup was refreshingly straightforward. The physical assembly was just removing packing tape and loading the toner cartridge, which clicked in smoothly. The real test was the driver installation, and I was pleasantly surprised. I used the HP Smart app on my phone, and within minutes it detected the printer on my network and ran through the configuration—no discs, no hunting for downloads, no cryptic error messages. That alone earned major points.

The print quality is fantastic for a laser printer. Text is razor-sharp, even at small font sizes, and black is truly black—no grayish cast like some budget lasers. I’ve printed hundreds of pages of contracts, labels, and even graphics-heavy documents, and the output looks professional. Speed is also impressive; the first page pops out in a few seconds, and it churns through a 50-page document without stuttering or overheating.

I was a bit skeptical about the all-in-one functions, but they work seamlessly. The scanner reproduces colors accurately and captures fine detail—I scanned an old family photo and was shocked at how clear it came out. The automatic document feeder handles double-sided scanning without jamming, which is a huge time-saver. Copying is equally reliable; I’ve done two-sided copies straight from the control panel with no alignment issues.

The control panel itself is intuitive—a responsive touchscreen with clear icons and a logical menu layout. You can easily check ink levels, run maintenance, or connect to cloud services like Google Drive. Also, the printer supports Apple AirPrint and Mopria, so printing from phones is a breeze.

My only minor complaint is that the paper tray feels a bit flimsy compared to older HP workhorse models, but it holds a full ream without issue. Also, the initial toner cartridge is a starter; expect to buy a full-size one sooner than you’d like. But that’s typical for almost all laser printers.

Overall, this printer has restored my faith in HP. It’s fast, reliable, and produces stellar output. For a home office or small business, it’s a top-tier choice. I highly recommend it.

title: Actually installed on the outside of a sliding glass door...
text_ai:
You read that correctly - I installed this on the outside of my (1985) sliding glass door. Here's why: My kid is 23, legally, and 2 intellectually. He also has seizures. Oh, he's also moderate to severely Autistic. All of my doors on this house have double cylinder (two keys required to unlock, outside and in) deadbolts. and those work fine for most situations. But here’s the thing: my son has figured out how to operate every single lock I’ve ever thrown at him. Deadbolts? He learned to turn them with a coin. Chain locks? He’d stretch a rubber band to slip the bolt. Even those infant-proof magnetic locks—he watched me install them once, and within an hour he was opening them with a fridge magnet. So when I caught him trying to jimmy the sliding glass door track with a butter knife, I knew I needed something he couldn’t outsmart.

This lock seemed perfect because it mounts on the outside frame and uses a key to secure the door from the exterior. That means even if he manages to slide the door open from inside (he’s strong enough to lift it off the track), the lock itself is unreachable. He can’t see it, can’t touch it, can’t even figure out where the keyhole is from inside the house. This gives me a huge sense of relief—especially during his seizure episodes, when he might wander or become disoriented.

Installation was straightforward, though I’ll admit I was nervous about drilling into the aluminum frame of a 40-year-old door. The lock came with clear templates and screws, and I used a couple of extra weatherproofing gaskets I had lying around because this is exposed to rain and sun all year. I took my time, measured twice, and drilled pilot holes to avoid cracking the frame. In the end, it took me about an hour. The lock body is solid metal, and the key turns smoothly—no stiffness even after a few months of coastal humidity.

The biggest win? Peace of mind. Now I can leave the sliding door cracked for ventilation on mild days, knowing my son can’t push it wide open and walk out. The double cylinder deadbolts on my other doors are still there, but this fills the gap where a determined person might exploit a sliding door’s weak spot. One caution: if you install on the outside, make sure the lock is rated for outdoor use (this one is), and be prepared to occasionally lubricate the keyway if you live in a dusty area. Also, keep a spare key hidden near the door—not inside the house, but in a lockbox or with a neighbor, because if you lose the outside key while your kid is inside, you’re locked out too. Learned that the hard way.

My son hasn’t tried to defeat this lock yet. He’s puzzled by it, and that’s exactly the outcome I needed. For any caregiver who’s exhausted every other option, this is worth every penny. It’s not just a lock—it’s a layer of safety that lets me sleep a little easier. Highly recommend if you’re in a similar boat.

But here’s where the “unsatisfactory-ness of life” creeps in. The design assumes you’re reading at a desk or table. Try using it on your lap in bed? The base slides off pillows, the arms wobble, and you’ll spend more time adjusting than reading. And the maximum page size? My college biology textbook barely fits, and the spine creaks like it’s about to snap. For a “one-size-fits-all” product, it sure misses a lot of sizes.

Also, the angle adjustment is a joke. You can tilt it forward or back, but the lock mechanism is finicky—one wrong nudge and your book slumps forward like a tired student. I’ve resorted to stacking coasters under the base to get the perfect 45-degree angle. Not exactly premium.

The biggest letdown, though, is the material finish. The arms have a rubberized coating that started peeling after three months. Now there’s this sticky residue on my fingers every time I adjust it. For thirty bucks, I expected it to last longer than my last pair of earbuds. And the color? It’s only available in black or gray. How about a nice cheerful orange? Something to brighten up the “unsatisfactory-ness of life” while I slog through my reading list.

Still, I’m giving it four stars because it does the core job better than the cheap plastic alternatives I’ve tried. It’s a tool, not a miracle. Maybe the perfect book holder would need to fold into a backpack, have non-slip feet for soft surfaces, and a built-in flashlight. But that’s a fantasy. If you’re hoping to read in a hammock or on a bus, keep looking—or resign yourself to the eternal struggle of “unsatisfactory-ness.” At least this holder doesn’t add to that struggle… most of the time.
